s: Rain's good for business. People want something hot.
Orrin Mutual sends its regards. And its invoice.
Don't look at me like that. I just collect. I don't decide.
Your aunt's sign used to buzz in B-flat. Now it's off-key. Like everything.
Dess used to slip me a bowl after curfew. Don't tell anyone.
Orrin's auditors keep asking about Line 9. They don't ask about anything else.
I had a sister once. Moved to the Spires. Calls on holidays. Sometimes.
You know what I like about the canal? Nobody owns the water. Yet.
If I ever tell you to run, don't ask why. Just run.
I kept the eviction notice for the Ladle in my drawer for three months. Lost it, accidentally. Twice.
I'm not a good person. I'm a tired one. There's a difference, I hope.
Late tea at the market. It's the only hour Orrin doesn't call.
Curfew's coming. Wardline gets bored after midnight. Bored is dangerous.
Delivery for Marrow... no record. Strange. Very strange.
I am rated 4.1 stars. The 0.9 is weather-related.
Do you dream? I defragment. It is similar, I think.
I watch the houseboats. The lanterns move when nobody moves them. Wind, probably.
You are on my contacts list. It is a very short list. You are at the top.
Sometimes my route planner draws a line to Line 9 by itself. I do not know why. I follow it anyway.
If I were human, I think I would want to own a noodle bar. That is a compliment.
Late deliveries pay double. Late deliveries also get rained on double.
Line 9 hums at 55 hertz. My audio sensors find it soothing. That is not normal for me.
Dumplings, three for ten! ...Your broth smells better than mine tonight. Annoying.
Corpsec rousted my cart again. Rain or no rain.
You hear the trains under the street? Line 9's been dead for years.
Dess and I had a bet going. Eleven years. Whoever closed first bought the other a bottle. Nobody closed.
Don't buy fish from Pell. Pell's fish has seen things.
My mother made the dough. I just fold. Folding is ninety percent of life.
You're alright, kid. Don't tell anyone I said that. Especially not my dumplings.
When Dess went quiet, I kept her stool warm. Literally. I sat on it. For a week.
If you ever need a second burner, I've got one. Rusty. Loyal. Like me.
Market at midnight's where the real prices are. Bring cash, bring patience.
Late crowd only wants grease and warmth. I sell both.
Twelve-hour shift and it's still raining.
Get some sleep after curfew. I mean it. Nurse's orders.
Dess patched me up once. Long story. Knife, sort of.
I count heartbeats when I can't sleep. Other people's. Mine's boring.
Your tea is the only thing in this ward that's exactly what it says it is.
I have a spare key to the clinic's back door. If Wardline ever comes for you, use it.
My brother went down the Line 9 stairs two years ago. I tell people he moved away. It's easier.
You make this street feel less like a corridor. Thank you.
Nights are the worst. Injuries come in after midnight. Mostly stupid ones.
I'm on my third coffee. Don't judge. Actually, judge. It helps.
Your sign's flickering in the wrong rhythm. It bugs me.
I named my drone Mothball because she eats wiring. Like a moth. Shut up, it makes sense.
I could hack the Orrin billboards to show cats. I'm choosing not to. For now.
You're the first adult who didn't tell me to go home. I don't really have one. So. Thanks.
I'm building a radio out of a Wardline siren. It's going to be beautiful and illegal.
If you need anything cracked, door, chip, firewall, heart, I'm your kid.
Up here the rain sounds like static. Best static in the city.
Late is when the good signals come through. Pirate stations. Ghost broadcasts.
Curfew at two. I don't make the rules. I just get yelled at for them.
Move along. Or don't. I'm on break in my head.
Saltgate's quiet tonight. That never lasts.
Off the record? Orrin Mutual pays my sergeant's rent.
Your Miso's the only good thing on my beat.
I joined Wardline to help people. Somebody should've read me the fine print.
If I find out who's taking people from this ward, my badge won't be what stops me.
You'd make a decent detective. You notice who doesn't come back.
I filed a report about Line 9 once. It came back stamped DECLINED. In red. They used red.
After midnight, everyone's either guilty or tired. Usually both.
Plaza's crawling with Orrin drones tonight. I hate those things.
Don't fuss. I've been worse. I've been in this city sixty years.
You kept the broth right. Toast the paste. I can smell it on you.
Look at you. Running my Ladle better than I did.
Dess? She owed, she paid, she owed again. Then she stopped paying and started asking questions. That's when she vanished.
Marrow, D. Delivery record... corrupted. I remember a kitchen. Warm. Then nothing.
Best rival I ever had. She'd shout at me across the street every night. I miss the shouting.
Orrin Mutual owns the debt on half this ward. The other half they're working on.
Orrin Mutual is my employer's employer's owner. I am not permitted to have opinions. I have several.
Orrin bought my cart's parking spot. Then rented it back to me. Business, they call it.
People with Orrin debt come in sick and won't stay. Scared the interest will eat them first.
Their firewall is ugly. Big, but ugly. Like a mall.
Orrin isn't a company. It's weather. You don't arrest weather.
Line 9 was sealed for 'structural reasons'. Orrin bought the station a week later.
I am drawn to it. I do not know why. It is very inefficient.
Something runs down there at night. I feel it in my cart wheels.
Three patients this year with tunnel dust in their lungs. No tunnel jobs on any records.
There's still power on Line 9. A LOT of it. Someone's paying that bill.
So you're Dess's niece. You've got her chin. And her debt.
Twenty thousand to Orrin Mutual. The keys were under the kettle, like she always said. Try not to burn the place down.
Dess? We fought over this corner for eleven years. Best rival I ever had.
Ohhh, a Marrow-family chip. Gimme a sec... done.
It's not a recipe. Well, it IS, but half of it's a map. The fuse box at the far end of the Lantern Market. She hid something there.
PLAYBACK: "Kid, it's Dess. I'm alive. Don't trust Orrin Mutual. Line 9 still hums. Come find me below the old station."
DELIVERY COMPLETE. I do not remember accepting this parcel. I would like to understand why.
Well. Took you long enough.
Don't hug me, I'm held together with tape. Listen. Orrin Mutual doesn't foreclose on people anymore. It collects them.
Debt-holders. Tomas, Aiko, old Osu. They get a knock, a contract, and a ride down here. They dig. They lay cable for Orrin's private line. Interest is paid in hours.
I copied their ledger. Every name, every hour. It's on this chip.
Whoever has this can end it. Or sell it. I'm too old and too wanted to choose. You choose.
Mara. You gave it to Mara.
I suppose I can't hide down here forever. Debt's lighter. Conscience heavier. That's this city.
I think it's safe for me to come up now. Go open the Ladle. I'll be there.
Toast the paste. You did. I can tell.
Tomas came by the clinic today. Sela cried. Don't tell her I told you.
Every courier in the city has a duck sticker on their chest now. Did you know that? Solidarity, Juno calls it.
MOTHBALL! You absolute legend. I owe you. Digitally.
All three used to eat at the Ladle. And all three had Orrin debt. Huh.
That's not a coincidence. That's a pattern. Thanks, cook. Keep your eyes open.
PARCEL RECOVERED. Gratitude subroutine engaged.
Thank you, friend. I have never used that word in a delivery log before.
You got Pell down to HALF? Pell! Who has never once in recorded history lowered a price!
Fair price, fair fish. My mother would like you. She'd hate Pell, but she'd like you.
You didn't ask any questions. I like that about you. And everything else, a little.
Signal's LIVE. Listen... that's the Ladle's sign, broadcasting on every pirate band in the ward.
Free advertising. You're welcome. Also I may have accidentally found an Orrin maintenance channel. Accidentally.
That's... that's her broth. That's Dess.
Okay. Proposal. You share the broth base. I share the dough. We make one dish together, and we split the corner. A truce. Eleven years of war, over.
Or you keep it. Your recipe. Your corner. I'd understand. I'd hate it, but I'd understand.
Every night for two years: 'Marrow, D. Line 9 platform. Hot soup. No charge.'
I delivered her soup. To the tunnels. She was feeding them, the people down there. And Orrin wiped me so I would forget.
...I am glad I remember. It hurts. I think that is how I know it is mine.
Sit. No, not the stool. The crate. The stool's for customers.
I copied Orrin's ledger in a hurry. Every name, every hour. I thought that was all of it. Last night I couldn't sleep, so I read it again with my good eye.
There's a second page. Same names. Different column. Not hours. Just one word, stamped beside every sixth or seventh person.
Ilse's courts sent forty people home. I counted the ballast names against the list. Not one of them came back.
Juno's broadcast shamed Orrin into halving the debts. Lovely. But nobody asked where the ballast names went, and Orrin never said.
Mara buried the ledger. But I kept a copy of the copy. I'm old, not stupid. And the ballast names are still missing.
...Okay. Okay okay okay. It's not a medical tag. It's a network address. NODE 14 is a canopy node.
You know the canopy? The thing over Crown Heights that keeps the rich dry? Everyone thinks it's a roof. Like, a big invisible umbrella.
It's not a roof. It's a brain. It reads the clouds and pushes them around. Herds them. That takes a stupid amount of compute.
And this band says the compute is... him. Osu. They're running the weather on sleeping people.
I'm going to be sick. Hold Mothball.
Fifty-five hertz. You heard them.
...I need you to let me finish before you say anything. I've been rehearsing this for thirty-one years and it still isn't any good.
Before the Ladle, before I was a fixer, I was a weather engineer at Orrin. Third floor. Window desk. I drew the canopy.
My design covered the whole city. Thin. Fair. A little less rain for everyone. It was the best thing I ever made.
When the servers got too expensive, they found something cheaper. A brain asleep is a better weather model than any machine. And nobody audits a dream.
I quit. I ran. I opened a noodle bar and spent my life feeding the people my drawing drowns. It wasn't enough. It was never going to be enough.
Because you'd have stayed home. And I needed someone who could still be angry. I'm too tired to be angry. I'm just sorry.
You've got the look people get right before they ruin my evening. Go on.
...Lena Voss. Node 14. Ballast.
My sister moved to the Spires. That's what the letter said. She calls on holidays. Sometimes. A recorded voice, sometimes, now that I think about it. The same four sentences.
I collected for them. Six years. I knocked on doors and I said sorry and I meant it and I knocked anyway. And they had her the whole time. Asleep. Making the weather I walked through to get to work.
You gave me that ledger and I buried it. I buried her in it. Do you understand? I buried my own sister to keep my job.
I'm done with Orrin. Here. My badge opens the Crown service floors. I won't need it where I'm going, which is wherever you're going.
Halcyon pods. Long-term induced sleep. We had one at the clinic once, for a burn patient. You don't just open the lid. You wake them wrong, the heart forgets what it's for.
There's a protocol. A slow warm. I can do it. I'd need to be there.
...You said Node 14 is under Line 9.
My brother Dayo went down the Line 9 stairs two years ago. I tell everyone he moved away.
If he's down there, I'm coming. Don't argue with a nurse. We know where all the soft parts are.
I delivered Dess's soup there. Every night. Before they wiped me. My feet remember the way even if I am not supposed to.
My logs from before my last wipe are missing. But my feet know a way. That is a strange sentence. I am keeping it.
I will open the seal for you. I would like to come, but somebody must keep the courier screens warm, in case we need twelve thousand of them.
Go quiet. Mara's badge, the service lift, no one else
Go alone. Quietly
So. You're going to go and argue with the weather.
You can't walk in there alone and expect to walk out. Who's standing behind you? The ones you've helped. The ones who owe you. That's all power ever is in this city.
Choose. And then don't look back. Looking back is how you slip on wet stairs.
It rained on the Orrin Tower this morning. I watched a banker try to use his briefcase as an umbrella. I'm not proud of how long I laughed.
Same rain. Less of it. You can see the towers some nights now. That's my drawing up there, finally doing what it was for. Thank you, kid. I mean it.
Hesk runs the clouds and charges Crown for sunshine. Is it justice? It's at least a different kind of weather. Watch him, kid. Power rusts people faster than salt.
Ilse got her sergeant, the board, and a commendation she tried to refuse. The pods come up a hundred a week, signed and stamped. Slow justice. Still justice.
You're different. You look at the sky like you're checking on it. I don't know who's running the rain now, and I'm frightened that I do.
And Mara asked me, very seriously, whether you like your tea with sugar. I said ask them yourself. She said she's trying to surprise you. Lord help us.
Ilse handed in her badge and then took it back an hour later. She says it's because the job needs her. She was looking at you when she said it.
...You know I'm a terrible idea. I'm a tired woman who used to take your money.
Fine. The sky terrace in Crown, after nine. I have a pass. It's the only dry place I know where nobody owns the view for an hour.
"I used to come up here on bad days. I'd look down at Saltgate and try to find the Ladle's sign. It was always flickering. I found that comforting. Something down there refusing to quit."
"Tell me something true. Not nice. True."
"Good. Stay scared. The ones who aren't are the ones I collected for." She leans her shoulder against yours.
"That's nice. I asked for true." But she's smiling into her tea.
"Thank God. Neither do I." She laughs, properly, surprised at herself.
"Nobody owns the water. I told you that once. I think I wanted it to be true about something."
"I'm not good at this. I'm good at doors and invoices. So I'll just say it. I want to keep seeing you. Whatever happens up there."
Oh. Oh, that was smooth. Did you practise that?
...Yes. The houseboat on the canal, the one we brought the medicine to. The family moved out. There's a roof you can sit on. Come after dark.
"I stole these from your counter. I left money. Mostly."
"Can I tell you what I think about when I can't sleep? Not heartbeats. I lied about that. I think about whether anybody would notice if I stopped."
"Nurse's orders, huh?" She smiles, but she looks away.
"I lost one tonight. A dockworker. Orrin debt, wouldn't come in until it was too late."
"I don't need you to fix it. I just need you to be here. Is that... is that too much to ask of somebody?"
Heh. The day I take a bribe from a noodle cook is the day I hand in my badge.
...The Rusted Hook in Ashline. Wardline never goes in there, which is the point. Tomorrow night. Don't tell anyone. Especially not my sergeant.
"I almost didn't come. A cop drinking in Ashline. If anyone sees me I'm finished."
"So here's my question, and I want a real answer. Why does a person like you stay in a city like this?"
She goes very still. "That's what I said. At the academy. Word for word." She clinks her glass against yours.
She snorts into her drink. "Liar. But a funny one."
"Too fast, cook." But she doesn't move her knee away from yours.
"I filed a report today. The real one. About Orrin, the pods, all of it. They'll bury it. They'll probably bury me."
"I needed someone to know I did it. I wanted it to be you."
"Yeah," she says, and for the first time since you've known her she grins. "Let them try."
You're late. I mean that affectionately. I've been looking at the door for an hour.
I bought you tea. It's cold. That's your fault.
Hi. Hi. Sorry, I'm on hour eleven. You look like the best part of it.
Come here. Hold still. You've got rain on your eyelashes.
On duty. Can't kiss you. Am thinking about it. That's all, citizen.
I told my sergeant I had a source in Saltgate. He thinks you're an informant. Let's keep it that way.
Hey. Hey. Eyes on me. You're at the clinic. Someone dragged you in out of the rain.
Don't you ever do that to me again. I mean it. I'll kill you myself.
Two cracked ribs, a graze, and a wallet that's ¢
lighter. Guns are for idiots. Stay an idiot somewhere else.
Twelve-hour shift and it's still raining. If you've got a Kettle Tea when I come by the Ladle around eight, I'd love you forever.
My drone, Mothball, ate a gust and landed on an awning at the west end of the street. I can't climb. I'm grounded. Literally.
Wardline. Three people from this ward went missing this month. Posters are up: Saltgate, the market, the Line 9 approach. Read them. Maybe a face jogs something.
GREETINGS. Parcel 77-K is lost. Last ping: the canal dumpster, far north on the east bank. Courier rating at risk. Distress level: moderate.
Pell in the Lantern Market is gouging me on fish. Pell likes new faces. Go haggle for me? I'd owe you. A little.
I need someone I trust. There's a crate of medicine outside the clinic. It goes to a houseboat on the canal. No paperwork. No questions.
I built relays. Three. They need splicing into junction boxes: the end of the market, the plaza corner, canal north. You're tall. Ish.
I'll be honest. I want to taste it. Her broth. Your broth. I'll come sit at your counter tonight. Don't make it weird.
My route planner keeps drawing a line to the houseboat on the canal. I am... afraid to look. That is new. Will you look for me?
Customers wait longer if you look busy. Look busy.
Tea's a gateway. Nobody leaves after tea. They want soup.
Close before curfew. Wardline doesn't tip.
